summary.text: Take the index \(27\): for every \(k\ge2\), \(k^{27}-27=(k^9-3)(k^{18}+3k^9+9)\), with both factors greater than \(1\), while \(k=0,1\) cannot yield a nonnegative prime, so no prime of the required form exists. Thus the value is \(0\) at \(27\), yet \(27\) is not the square of an even integer.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S_n=\{p\in\mathbb N: p\text{ is prime and }b^n=p+n\text{ for some }b\in\mathbb N\}.
\]
Thus \(a(n)\) is the least element of \(S_n\), with the stipulated value \(a(n)=0\) when \(S_n\) is empty. We will show that \(S_{27}\) is empty, although \(27\) is not the square of an even integer. This gives the required counterexample.

We first prove that no prime can have the form \(b^{27}-27\). Suppose, toward a contradiction, that there are natural numbers \(b,p\) such that \(p\) is prime and
\[
b^{27}=p+27. \tag{1}
\]
We divide the argument according as \(b\ge 2\) or \(b<2\).

Assume first that \(b\ge 2\). Then \(b^9\ge 2^9=512\), so in particular \(b^9\ge 3\), and the following difference-of-cubes factorization involves only nonnegative integers:
\[
\begin{aligned}
b^{27}-27
  &= (b^9)^3-3^3\\
  &= (b^9-3)\bigl((b^9)^2+3b^9+3^2\bigr)\\
  &= (b^9-3)(b^{18}+3b^9+9).
\end{aligned} \tag{2}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
b^{27}=(b^9-3)(b^{18}+3b^9+9)+27. \tag{3}
\]
Comparing (1) and (3), and cancelling the added \(27\), gives
\[
p=(b^9-3)(b^{18}+3b^9+9). \tag{4}
\]
Set
\[
A=b^9-3,\qquad B=b^{18}+3b^9+9.
\]
Then \(A\mid p\). Since \(p\) is prime, every natural-number divisor of \(p\) is either \(1\) or \(p\). We consider these two possibilities.

If \(A=1\), then \(b^9-3=1\), so \(b^9=4\). But \(b\ge2\) implies \(b^9\ge512\), a contradiction.

If \(A=p\), then (4) becomes
\[
p=pB.
\]
A prime is positive, so cancellation of the positive factor \(p\) yields \(B=1\). This is also impossible, since
\[
B=b^{18}+3b^9+9\ge9>1.
\]
Thus (1) cannot hold when \(b\ge2\).

It remains to consider \(b<2\). Since \(b\) is a natural number, there are exactly two cases.

* If \(b=0\), then (1) says \(0=p+27\), impossible because \(p+27\ge27>0\).
* If \(b=1\), then (1) says \(1=p+27\), impossible because again \(p+27\ge27\).

Consequently there are no natural numbers \(b,p\) with \(p\) prime and \(b^{27}=p+27\). Hence
\[
S_{27}=\varnothing,
\]
and by the definition of the sequence in the empty case,
\[
a(27)=0. \tag{5}
\]

Finally, \(27\) is not the square of an even integer. Indeed, for every \(m\in\mathbb N\),
\[
(2m)^2=4m^2
\]
is divisible by \(4\), whereas \(27\equiv3\pmod4\). Therefore
\[
27\ne(2m)^2
\]
for every natural number \(m\).

Thus the index \(27\) satisfies \(a(27)=0\) but is not the square of an even integer. It is therefore a counterexample to the conjecture that every \(k\) with \(a(k)=0\) must be of the form \((2m)^2\).
